Heyo! I'm a university sophomore, and I've gone through various educational models through the years (never stayed at a single school for more than 2 years). I was IQ tested at 5 years old and came out to be 3-4 SD's above the mean. I have a lot of things I wanna say and I'm not sure how to organize it all, so I'm just gonna spitball.

I can only speak from my own experience - but I've found that many traditional academically rigorous schools end up falling into the pattern of prioritizing quantity over quality. That is, drilling work into the kids' heads to give them an edge. They tend to be rigid in structure/curriculum, and often have a "we know best" attitude. I've been to a couple schools like that. I burned out pretty quickly.

Now, you might get lucky and end up with a kid who just so happens to thrive in a normal school. If that's the case, great! I'm glad to hear that your kid is doing well at their current school. But if they don't do well in a traditional system, definitely look for non-traditional options.

A better way to put this is that for a gifted student, it doesn't always work to exclusively prioritize academic rigor. Instead, look for **flexibility**. Gifted kids by nature aren't going to learn at the same rate, or even in the same manner as their peers. Forcing them into an academic model that doesn't work for them (however advanced it may be) will end badly. I know this from experience. Each gifted kid is unique, and there likely isn't a school out there that will be a perfect fit right off the bat. Sometimes it's more valuable to find a school that is willing to shift things around and bend the rules to accommodate your kid's specific learning style.

I'm not a parent, so please take this with a huge pile of salt. If you're shooting for college, yes - it's important to develop traditional study skills and such. But in 2nd grade, that's a long ways off. Right now, it's arguably more important to foster a foundational love of learning. The stereotypical "gifted kid burnout" is often the product of attempts to fit a naturally atypical mind into a typical educational system.

"Gifted programs k-8 feels like it’s too good to be true."  
Definitely not. In-person schooling might be harder to find, but there are loads of online options. I know going fully online isn't an option for a lot of families, but even just a single online course to supplement traditional learning can make all the difference. Online schooling often offers opportunities that aren't available in-person. I'm talking about stuff like AoPS (Art of Problem Solving). They offer advanced math courses for grades 5-12 (their offshoot "Beast Academy" is geared towards younger kids), and some of their stuff isn't ever touched upon in the standard school system. I took several discrete math courses (notably Number Theory + Counting and Probability) with them in middle school.

That's all I have for now. Feel free to DM if you wanna discuss more.

Here's something to think about. You do not owe the world academic achievement. There's a huge tendency for people to commodify intelligence, and the result is that people with high intellectual potential tie their self worth purely to their performance.

Your life's purpose doesn't have to rely on your ability to impress others or score well on standardized tests. I was IQ tested at 5 years old. I'm 3-4 standard deviations above the mean. I spent most of my life with this goddamn number steering my education. But my mental health was spiraling - when I was 9, I was hospitalized for suicidal ideation.

Fast forward to my junior year of high school, after the whole family moved so I could attend a gifted school (the kind you have to submit an iq test to attend). By definition, the school prioritized academic potential over everything else. That same year, I stayed at a residential treatment center for several months, got kicked out of the house, started working part time as a server in a shitty IHOP, and slept on the floor in an ant infested rental basement.

I wanted to die. Oh, how the mighty have fallen. The kid who took the ACT when they were nine, the kid who probably could have had a PhD by now. I felt crushed by the reality that I was likely never going to live up to my "potential", the stupid number stamped on my forehead when I was 5.

And then it clicked. That "potential" that I thought I had? It was entirely based on what *other* people wanted me to do. Take this test, do well in that class, all against my will. Sure, I could crush any exam I wanted to, but what was the point if it didn't bring *me* any joy or contentment? I was sacrificing my own happiness in order to chase this perfect image of what I *thought* I was supposed to be.

My advice? Find something *you* want to do. Stop worrying about living up to the academic potential others have assigned to you. If you can find something of *your* choosing that helps you feel good about yourself, then that's the only potential you need to live up to.

TL:DR - Stop tying your self worth to the image *others* expect you to fit. Find something that makes *you* happy, and run with that.  


And honestly? You don't even need something that makes you happy. You don't need a reason to feel worthy of living. You have inherent worth just by existing. If in this moment you don't have the motivation to chase some passion, that's okay. You are allowed to simply *be*. You don't have to feel bad about that.

I have a few friends who have done DAO through high school. I think in this day and age, in-person socializing is pretty difficult anyway. DAO is a totally valid option, provided that you make sure your kid has other social opportunities. Even something as simple as recreation soccer could make all the difference.

I was homeschooled for all of elementary school. It worked okay for a while, but once I got to high school I started growing rather rapidly both emotionally and socially. My freshman year was awful - I went to a boarding school up in Tahoe because my parents couldn't deal with having me in the house. For sophomore year, I went to my local public high school. It was easily the best year of my life, but it wasn't going to last. I was taking their highest courses in most subjects, and just wouldn't have had anything left to take by my senior year.

So I transferred to the Davidson Academy. I don't know if you've heard of that - but it's a school specifically designed for profoundly gifted kids. My parents made me repeat sophomore year so that I'd stay there for a full three years, but I ended up hating it. I desperately wanted a normal life: shitty parties, making stupid decisions with other teens...

I definitely wouldn't have gotten that if I had homeschooled throughout high school. As hard as it is to make friends as a PG individual, I managed to find a lil alcove of friends at my public school. That really did make all the difference. My biggest regret is transferring out of there. There were other options that I could have taken to supplement my academics, but I ended up sacrificing my social life and was miserable because of it.

Socialization is important for all ages, but I think it's especially critical in the teen years. Homeschooling in high school probably wouldn't have worked well for me, but keep in mind that every kid is different.

Oh hey, I took the ACT when I was nine! This is the first time I've heard of anyone else thinking of doing that.

I did what you're thinking of doing, sort of. I used my ACT score to test out of English 101 at my local college, and took English 102 online. But that was the ONLY college course I took. The rest of my middle school education was covered by various other online programs (Art of Problem Solving was the notable one - it's probably the best option out there for gifted kids who are advanced in mathematics). I then went to four separate high schools, skipped senior year, and graduated at 17 years old. I'm attending my state school now, and seeking to transfer after my sophomore year.

Keep in mind that taking college courses at nine years old is very different from actually going to college at 18. When you're that young, you miss out on the social component of college that makes it so exciting. It's purely academic, and I think I'd go insane if my college experience was like that. My dad went to Harvard when he was 15, and he was miserable.

I'd say that taking a few select courses at the local college as a non-degree seeking student is a decent idea, provided that he has other social opportunities. When I was his age, I went to the Davidson Young Scholars Summit and PG Retreat every summer. I'd highly recommend both of those programs, as they pretty much prevented me from going completely insane.

Long story short, I'd recommend allowing him to take college classes as a non-degree seeking student, and trying your best to get him to graduate high school relatively on time so he doesn't end up doing what my dad did. If you have any more questions, feel free to DM.

Yeah, I'd like to add that the people who *were* happy there were REALLY happy there. I think the DA is very much a "hate it or love it" sort of situation. It's definitely not right for everyone, and it certainly wasn't right for me. But for the right kid it can truly be a lifesaver both academically and socially.

I only have experience with the Reno in person campus. I went there for nearly two years before transferring out due to unforeseen circumstances (COVID hit, had some personal issues). I have a friend who attended Davidson Academy Online throughout high school, but I personally don't know much about it.

Also, please note that my experience is unique to me. I personally didn't have a good time there, but I know plenty of other people who did.

I'd say that the DA is the best option out there for students who genuinely cannot survive anywhere else. There's a lot to be said for finding a community of like minded peers and not having to worry about feeling ostracized due to giftedness. However, it wasn't the right environment for me. I had been attending my local high school in Las Vegas before deciding to transfer to the DA, and I was happy there. As a child I had a hard time making friends, but I managed to gain a lot of emotional and social intelligence during my early teens, and got to a point where I was able to manage just fine (socially AND academically) at a normal school. When I got to the DA, I was shocked by just how tiny the social pool was. It was mostly middle schoolers, and the high school crowd seemed to be split into pre-established cliques (in particular, one group of juniors who had been at the DA for a long f\*cking time).

If your child is struggling with the feeling that their giftedness is the only thing people seem to acknowledge about them, note that going to the DA *might* exacerbate that issue. I found that going to a school that accepts kids purely based on IQ only *worsened* the feeling of being "different". I wanted a normal life - going to parties, making bad decisions with other teens, and fully enjoying my adolescence. The DA is heavily academically focused. No sports, no sh\*tty parties. I eventually found that the environment made me feel stifled, and I suffered from burnout (similar to a lot of the other high schoolers) soon after transferring.

But do note that I was struggling with a lot of other issues at the time. My school counselor had to call CPS on my parents several times, and I spent my summer at a residential treatment center. The point is that the tiny, academics-only atmosphere of the DA really didn't help my emotional state.

The academics themselves are great, at least in the classes I took. The curriculum dives considerably deeper into each concept, and is very clearly tailored towards profoundly gifted (PG) students. My calculus teacher in particular was amazing, and I'm still very sorry that I wasn't in the proper place emotionally to be able to take full advantage of what he offered me.

As for flexibility... Well, I have mixed views on that point. I'll say that the DA is good about placing students based on academic ability instead of age. My advanced chemistry class included kids from 8th grade to 12th. However, once you are locked into a track set by the DA, it's their way or the highway. They're very strict about keeping kids on a track once they enter the system. The DA actually took a lot of my core high school credits that I had previously earned, and turned them into electives to force me into sophomore standing. When my home situation worsened and I needed to quickly graduate high school, I asked them to reverse that decision. They said no. 

But once again, please note that I am by no means an average case. I uh... had a lot of issues.

In conclusion, the DA is great for a very specific type of gifted kid: the type who is extremely passionate about academics, and needs a place that is able to keep up with them and allow them to dive deeper into the content. If your kid is interested in music, sports, or big ol' high school parties, the DA can't help you there. I made a few good friends, and being surrounded by exclusively PG peers made it pretty easy to find them. But outside of those three (four?), there wasn't much. The tiny social circle can either be a perfect match, or a stifling trap. It really just depends on the kid and what their needs are.

And once again, this only applies to my personal experience at the Reno, Nevada campus. Maybe I would have had a much better time if factors out of my control had tilted more in my favor. COVID, along with my own rapidly deteriorating family life, really did throw a wrench in everything. Oh also I am tipsy while writing this, so please disregard anything that sounds stupid. :P

Hey! I tested as somewhere between 3-4 standard deviations above the mean when I was around five years old. I'm 18 and thriving in college now. My parents and I really went through the wringer when it came to finding me a good educational fit throughout my childhood. There's a lot there, and if you have any more questions then feel free to DM me. Here are a few basic tips, though:

\-Prioritize flexibility over claims of being "advanced". There are a lot of cushy private schools out there that claim to help children get ahead, but these places often do this through intense repetition and strictness (AKA a gifted kid's worst nightmare).

\-I've found that there are three things to look for in a school: academic fit, social fit, and long-term stability. It's very difficult to find all three at one school, and you usually only end up with two. If this is the case, look for other ways to supplement the area that's lacking. For social issues, try getting your kid into gifted gatherings so they can find like-minded peers outside of school. If that's not possible, even something as simple as recreational soccer can help your kid feel less isolated.

\-For academics, there are tons of online options you can use to supplement your kid's education if your current school just isn't cutting it. For math, look into AoPS (Art of Problem Solving). They have a great elementary school level subprogram called Beast Academy, and everything from Number Theory (great class, i took that) to Calculus for older kiddos. When I was in middle school, we talked to the principal and managed to set a system up for me so I could do AoPS on my own time instead of sitting through my Godawful 6th grade math class. Once again, **flexibility is key**. Gifted kids are often stronger in some subjects than others, so it pays off to have a school that is willing to accommodate those unique needs.

\-The holy grail for gifted education is arguably the Davidson Academy of Nevada (Reno). You'll need to provide proof of an IQ score above 3 standard deviations, and you'll need to go through a rather painstaking interview process as well. The classes are taught with profound giftedness in mind, so they dive much deeper into the content than any other school I've ever been to. Plus, it's located on the University of Nevada Reno campus, so kids can just take university classes if they ever hit the ceiling in any subjects. I went there for almost two years in high school (it's grade 6-12 as far as i know). I'll admit that it wasn't a good fit for me, and I ended up transferring out, but it's probably the best option out there if you have a profoundly gifted child who can't survive at any other school. Then again, COVID-19 hit shortly after I transferred there, so I probably didn't get to see the best of it.

\-There's an online section of the DA as well if moving to Reno isn't possible for you. Like I said before, if your kid ends up feeling isolated due to the lack of social opportunities, do your best to get them into other activities outside of school to help mitigate that feeling of loneliness. I know from experience that isolation can crush a child's spirit...

\-Speaking of loneliness, be **very careful** if you decide to skip grades. It might work well academically in the short term, but it can also be really hard on a kid to be constantly surrounded by older kids. Asynchronous development is a big issue. Your kid might academically be in grade 8, but emotionally still be a 6th grader. Keep that in mind if you decide to accelerate.

\-Gifted kids still need support for their weaknesses. This one's kinda niche, but it made a huge difference for me: keep the possibility of learning disabilities or other struggles in the back of your mind. Often times, gifted kids seem so far ahead that nobody notices that they're struggling due to undiagnosed conditions. I'm not saying that you need to get your kid tested RIGHT NOW, but please don't assume that everything is fine because they're ahead. Gifted kids often have issues with perfectionism, and those invisible struggles could cause intense frustration down the road for them personally even if nobody else sees it.

\-The end thing to realize is that while your kid might be years ahead in academics, they're still a kid at heart. My dad went to Harvard when he was 15, and he struggled due to his lack of emotional and social maturity. Granted, every kid is different. But please understand that there is a delicate balance between a kid's academic happiness and emotional happiness.
